title: Which interventions bring a polarized society back together, and does contact backfire?
summary: 1,000 simulated people in two camps (opinions near 0.2 and 0.8, 95% of ties within camp) follow bounded confidence (Deffuant et al. 2000) with optional repulsion from distant views (Jager & Amblard 2005); the model reproduces Deffuant’s floor(1/(2ε)) cluster count and the Hegselmann–Krause consensus threshold. Six levers are swept over dose, tolerance ε 0.2–0.4 and rejection threshold τ (none, 0.9–0.6), 10 societies each. Rewiring ties across camps never merges them below ε = 0.4 and is the only lever that backfires: at τ = 0.7, rewiring 10% of ties sends everyone to the extremes (10% with no lever). Over 25 settings at top dose, a ladder of committed voices merges the camps in 24, a moderate broadcast or committed moderates in 19, a one-off nudge in 14, raising tolerance in 8 and bridging in 2 (more people at the extremes in 10). A ladder must be spaced for the least tolerant: built for ε = 0.3 when the real one is 0.2, it merges none of 10. Tolerance, rejection threshold and the network are not measured for any real population and are swept, not sourced; opinions are one-dimensional and contact here changes positions only, not prejudice. Includes an interactive browser simulator.
lede: which interventions bring a polarized society back together? In an opinion-dynamics model with backfire swept from none to strong, bridging ties across camps never merges them and at a rejection threshold of 0.7 rewiring 10% of ties drives everyone to the extremes, while a ladder of committed voices within reach merges them in 24 of 25 settings (moderate broadcast 19, nudge 14, tolerance 8, bridging 2); interactive simulator included (tolerance and backfire are swept, not measured).
